items.stem: State what is meant by the term "mitigation".
items.answer: Action to reduce or prevent greenhouse-gas emissions or enhance sinks, reducing the scale of climate change
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: action to reduce or prevent greenhouse-gas emissions or enhance sinks, reducing the scale of climate change. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Diego writes: "Carbon taxes always hurt the poor most." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They can be regressive, but revenue recycling (e.g. Canada's rebates) can leave most low-income households better off.
items.markingKey: They can be regressive, but revenue recycling (e.g. Canada's rebates) can leave most low-income households better off. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mitigation and adaptation.
items.answer: Mitigation tackles the causes of climate change by reducing emissions or increasing sinks; adaptation reduces the harm from climate impacts that cannot be avoided.
items.markingKey: Mitigation tackles the causes of climate change by reducing emissions or increasing sinks; adaptation reduces the harm from climate impacts that cannot be avoided. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The USA emitted about 4,900 Mt of CO₂ from fossil fuels in a recent year and has a population of about 335 million. Calculate the emissions per person.
items.answer: 4,900 / 335 = 14.63 t CO₂ per person
items.markingKey: M1 Mt ÷ million people = t per person; A1 14.63 t.

items.stem: Suggest why mitigation requires international rather than only national action.
items.answer: Greenhouse gases mix globally; one country's cuts can be offset by others' growth or carbon leakage; free-riding means coordinated agreements are needed.
items.markingKey: Greenhouse gases mix globally; one country's cuts can be offset by others' growth or carbon leakage; free-riding means coordinated agreements are needed.

items.stem: A cement plant covered by Sweden emits 605,000 t CO₂ per year. The carbon price is about SEK 1200 per tonne. Calculate the annual carbon cost, and the saving if the plant cuts emissions by 25%. Evaluate carbon pricing as a mitigation strategy.
items.answer: cost SEK 726,000,000; after cut SEK 544,500,000; saving SEK 181,500,000
items.markingKey: A1 SEK 726,000,000; M1 A1 saving SEK 181,500,000. R1 R1 incentive to cut emissions / revenue recycling vs carbon leakage, regressive impacts, prices often too low.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of two contrasting climate change mitigation strategies.
items.answer: Indicative content: Two named strategies with locations and data (e.g. Swedish carbon tax, EU ETS, Great Green Wall, Sleipner CCS, Costa Rica renewables); costs, benefits, scale; judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two named strategies with locations and data (e.g. Swedish carbon tax, EU ETS, Great Green Wall, Sleipner CCS, Costa Rica renewables); costs, benefits, scale; judgement. Paper 1 extended-response markbands [10]: 9-10 responds to all demands of the question; accurate, detailed knowledge and understanding; well-developed, relevant examples and case studies with specific (named, located, quantified) detail; balanced, well-structured evaluation leading to a substantiated conclusion. 7-8 responds to most demands; mostly accurate knowledge; examples relevant but not always fully developed; evaluation present but uneven. 5-6 some demands addressed; knowledge partly accurate; examples general or loosely linked; evaluation mostly implicit. 3-4 limited, largely descriptive; little use of examples. 1-2 little relevant knowledge or understanding. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: "Carbon taxes are the most effective mitigation strategy available to governments." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Carbon pricing is highly effective where politically sustainable, but it works best with regulation and public investment.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: Sweden shows strong reductions with growth; economists favour pricing for efficiency. Arguments challenging it: political resistance (France's gilets jaunes 2018); regressive effects and carbon leakage; regulation and investment also needed. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Carbon pricing is highly effective where politically sustainable, but it works best with regulation and public investment. Paper 2 Section C markbands [15]: 13-15 thorough response to all demands including the command term; accurate, detailed geographical knowledge and terminology; well-chosen, located and quantified examples at more than one scale; explicit, balanced evaluation (perspectives, places, scales, time) with a well-substantiated conclusion. 10-12 most demands addressed; accurate knowledge; examples relevant and developed; evaluation is balanced but not sustained. 7-9 some demands addressed; knowledge mostly accurate; examples partly developed; evaluation partial or one-sided. 4-6 limited, mainly descriptive; generalised examples; little evaluation. 1-3 little relevant knowledge; no examples or evaluation. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "emissions trading scheme"?
options: A cap-and-trade system in which a limit on emissions is set and permits are traded, e.g. the EU ETS (2005)
A charge on fossil fuels or emissions per tonne of CO₂, intended to make polluters pay and encourage low-carbon choices
Action to reduce or prevent greenhouse-gas emissions or enhance sinks, reducing the scale of climate change
Planting trees on land that has not recently been forested, to create carbon sinks
items.answer: A cap-and-trade system in which a limit on emissions is set and permits are traded, e.g. the EU ETS (2005)
items.markingKey: A. "emissions trading scheme" is a cap-and-trade system in which a limit on emissions is set and permits are traded, e.g. the EU ETS (2005).

items.stem: Briefly explain why geo-engineering is controversial.
items.answer: Solar radiation management could be cheap but does not cut CO₂ or acidification, may disrupt monsoons, creates a "termination shock" risk if stopped and raises governance questions about who controls the global thermostat.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Solar radiation management could be cheap but does not cut CO₂ or acidification, may disrupt monsoons, creates a "termination shock" risk if stopped and raises governance questions about who controls the global thermostat. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Felix writes: "Geo-engineering would solve climate change, so emissions cuts are unnecessary." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Solar geo-engineering would mask warming but not remove CO₂, leaving ocean acidification and the risk of rapid warming if it stopped.
items.markingKey: Solar geo-engineering would mask warming but not remove CO₂, leaving ocean acidification and the risk of rapid warming if it stopped. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Sleipner gas field, Norway, explain how it illustrates carbon capture and storage.
items.answer: About 1 million tonnes of CO₂ a year has been injected into a saline aquifer since 1996, encouraged by Norway's offshore carbon tax. CCS can work where there is a strong carbon price and suitable geology.
items.markingKey: Context (About 1 million tonnes of CO₂ a year has been injected into a saline aquifer since 1996, encouraged by Norway's offshore carbon tax.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: CCS can work where there is a strong carbon price and suitable geology. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to carbon capture and storage.

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Table: share of renewables in electricity generation (%, approximate recent year) - Costa Rica 99; Norway 98; Denmark 84; Germany 52; China 31; USA 22; Saudi Arabia 1.

Describe the variation shown.
items.answer: Very high shares in Costa Rica and Norway (hydro), high in Denmark (wind) and Germany, moderate in China and the USA, almost none in Saudi Arabia.
items.markingKey: Very high shares in Costa Rica and Norway (hydro), high in Denmark (wind) and Germany, moderate in China and the USA, almost none in Saudi Arabia. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Electricity generation in a sub-Saharan African country in one year: coal 69 TWh, natural gas 0 TWh, oil 38 TWh, nuclear 7 TWh, hydro 117 TWh, wind 60 TWh, solar 3 TWh. Calculate the percentage of electricity from renewable sources. Also calculate the share from fossil fuels and the share that is low-carbon (renewables + nuclear).
items.answer: Total 294 TWh; renewables 180 TWh = 61.2%; fossil 36.4%; low-carbon 63.6%
items.markingKey: M1 total 294 TWh; M1 renewables (hydro + wind + solar) 180; A1 61.2%. A1 fossil 36.4%; A1 low-carbon 63.6%.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Text: "Sweden's territorial greenhouse-gas emissions fell by about 33% between 1990 and 2020 while real GDP rose by about 80%." - Swedish Environmental Protection Agency summary.

(a) Describe what the data show about the relationship between growth and emissions. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest one limitation of using territorial emissions to judge Sweden's performance. [6]
items.answer: (a) Absolute decoupling: emissions fell substantially while GDP rose, showing growth does not require rising emissions. (b) It excludes emissions embedded in imported goods (consumption-based emissions) and international aviation and shipping.
items.markingKey: (a) Absolute decoupling: emissions fell substantially while GDP rose, showing growth does not require rising emissions. items.stem: Examine the view that technological solutions such as carbon capture and geo-engineering offer the best hope of mitigating climate change.
items.answer: Technology helps, but proven measures (renewables, efficiency, carbon pricing, forests) must lead; risky geo-engineering is not a substitute.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: net-zero pathways in IPCC scenarios include CO₂ removal; CCS can decarbonise cement and steel. Against / limitations: CCS is expensive and slow to scale; geo-engineering is risky and does not cut CO₂; renewables and efficiency are cheaper and available now. A supported conclusion might be: Technology helps, but proven measures (renewables, efficiency, carbon pricing, forests) must lead; risky geo-engineering is not a substitute. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "adaptation".
items.answer: Adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate change to reduce harm or exploit opportunities
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate change to reduce harm or exploit opportunities. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Building higher sea walls is always the best adaptation." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sea walls are expensive, can fail, push erosion elsewhere and encourage development in risky places (maladaptation); soft or nature-based options may be better.
items.markingKey: Sea walls are expensive, can fail, push erosion elsewhere and encourage development in risky places (maladaptation); soft or nature-based options may be better. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between top-down adaptation and bottom-up adaptation.
items.answer: Top-down adaptation is planned and funded by governments or international agencies; bottom-up adaptation is led by local communities using local knowledge.
items.markingKey: Top-down adaptation is planned and funded by governments or international agencies; bottom-up adaptation is led by local communities using local knowledge. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cooperative growing rice in Vietnam harvested 17,410 t from 5,918 ha in 2005 and 25,472 t from the same area in 2020. Calculate the yield (t/ha) in each year and the percentage change in yield.
Using Hulhumalé, Maldives as an example, explain land-raising as adaptation.
items.answer: A reclaimed island about 2 m above sea level, planned to house over 200,000 people. Creating higher land reduces exposure, though at high cost and environmental impact on reefs.
items.markingKey: Context (A reclaimed island about 2 m above sea level, planned to house over 200,000 people.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Creating higher land reduces exposure, though at high cost and environmental impact on reefs. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to land-raising as adaptation.

items.stem: Examine the view that community-based adaptation is more effective than large-scale engineering.
items.answer: The most effective approaches combine community action with appropriate infrastructure and state support.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: cheap, uses local knowledge, builds social capital (Bangladesh volunteers); avoids maladaptation. Against / limitations: some threats need large infrastructure (Dutch delta works, Thames Barrier); communities lack funds and technical capacity. A supported conclusion might be: The most effective approaches combine community action with appropriate infrastructure and state support. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "adaptation"?
options: A charge on fossil fuels or emissions per tonne of CO₂, intended to make polluters pay and encourage low-carbon choices
Non-governmental organisations, social movements, faith groups and individuals acting collectively outside government and business
Adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate change to reduce harm or exploit opportunities
An integrated system of hazard monitoring, forecasting, risk communication and preparedness that enables timely action
items.answer: Adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate change to reduce harm or exploit opportunities
items.markingKey: C. "adaptation" is adjustments in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climate change to reduce harm or exploit opportunities.

items.stem: Explain how mangrove restoration can build coastal resilience.
items.answer: Mangroves dissipate wave energy and storm surge, trap sediment that raises land, store carbon and support fisheries, as in Vietnam's Mekong delta and the Sundarbans.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mangroves dissipate wave energy and storm surge, trap sediment that raises land, store carbon and support fisheries, as in Vietnam's Mekong delta and the Sundarbans. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Adaptation means giving up on reducing emissions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adaptation and mitigation are complementary; both are needed because some impacts are already unavoidable.
items.markingKey: Adaptation and mitigation are complementary; both are needed because some impacts are already unavoidable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
The following information is provided.

Table: deaths from major cyclones in Bangladesh - Bhola 1970: about 300,000-500,000; 1991 cyclone: 138,000; Sidr 2007: about 4,200; Amphan 2020: 26.

Suggest two reasons for the trend.
items.answer: Improved forecasting and warnings through the Cyclone Preparedness Programme; thousands of cyclone shelters and embankments; better evacuation and community awareness.
items.markingKey: Improved forecasting and warnings through the Cyclone Preparedness Programme; thousands of cyclone shelters and embankments; better evacuation and community awareness. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (24.2 − 15.4) ÷ 15.4 × 100; A1 +57.1% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Infographic description: Rotterdam Climate Proof - Maeslantkering storm-surge barrier (1997, two 210 m gates); Benthemplein water square stores 1.7 million litres of storm water; 400,000+ m² of green roofs; floating pavilion.

(a) Classify the measures shown as hard or soft adaptation. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain how the water square reduces flood risk. [6]
items.answer: (a) Hard: the Maeslantkering barrier; multifunctional / green-blue infrastructure: water square, green roofs, floating buildings (soft or nature-based approaches). (b) It temporarily stores heavy rainfall (1.7 million litres), slowing runoff into sewers and preventing surface-water flooding, then releases it slowly.
items.markingKey: (a) Hard: the Maeslantkering barrier; multifunctional / green-blue infrastructure: water square, green roofs, floating buildings (soft or nature-based approaches). items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nationally determined contribution (NDC)"?
options: Large-scale deliberate intervention in the climate system, such as solar radiation management or ocean fertilisation
An action intended to reduce climate risk that increases vulnerability elsewhere or in the future, e.g. sea walls that encourage building in exposed areas
A country's self-set climate pledge under the Paris Agreement, to be updated and strengthened every five years
A charge on fossil fuels or emissions per tonne of CO₂, intended to make polluters pay and encourage low-carbon choices
items.answer: A country's self-set climate pledge under the Paris Agreement, to be updated and strengthened every five years
items.markingKey: C. "nationally determined contribution (NDC)" is a country's self-set climate pledge under the Paris Agreement, to be updated and strengthened every five years.

items.stem: Explain why the Paris Agreement achieved wider participation than the Kyoto Protocol.
items.answer: It is bottom-up: every country sets its own NDC, so developing countries such as China and India take part, whereas Kyoto set binding targets only for industrialised countries; flexibility made it acceptable to the USA and others.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is bottom-up: every country sets its own NDC, so developing countries such as China and India take part, whereas Kyoto set binding targets only for industrialised countries; flexibility made it acceptable to the USA and others. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The Paris Agreement legally requires each country to meet its emissions target." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: NDCs are not legally binding in content; the obligations are procedural - to prepare, communicate and report on them.
items.markingKey: NDCs are not legally binding in content; the obligations are procedural - to prepare, communicate and report on them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Between 2000 and 2010 the annual CO₂ emissions of a Gulf state changed from 395.7 to 475.3 Mt CO₂. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (475.3 − 395.7) ÷ 395.7 × 100; A1 +20.1% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
The following information is provided.

Table: projected warming by 2100 (UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2023) - current policies: about 2.9 °C; unconditional NDCs: 2.5 °C; conditional NDCs: 2.5 °C; net-zero pledges fully met: 1.9 °C.

Describe what the data show.
items.answer: Current policies would lead to about 2.9 °C; full delivery of all pledges would reduce warming to about 1.9 °C - still above 1.5 °C.
items.markingKey: Current policies would lead to about 2.9 °C; full delivery of all pledges would reduce warming to about 1.9 °C - still above 1.5 °C. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that international agreements have been ineffective in tackling climate change.
items.answer: Agreements have been insufficient but not ineffective; they have bent the curve and created frameworks for stronger action.
items.markingKey: For: global emissions have risen about 60% since 1990. Against: without agreements warming projections would be higher (about 4 °C pre-Paris). [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Define the term "UNFCCC".
items.answer: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, agreed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, which aims to stabilise greenhouse-gas concentrations at a safe level
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, agreed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, which aims to stabilise greenhouse-gas concentrations at a safe level. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-state actors in climate governance and state actors.
items.answer: State actors are national governments negotiating treaties; non-state actors include cities, businesses, NGOs and social movements that act and lobby independently.
items.markingKey: State actors are national governments negotiating treaties; non-state actors include cities, businesses, NGOs and social movements that act and lobby independently. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Individual protest has no effect on climate policy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Movements such as Fridays for Future and Extinction Rebellion have contributed to climate emergency declarations and policy debates.
items.markingKey: Movements such as Fridays for Future and Extinction Rebellion have contributed to climate emergency declarations and policy debates. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Recent fossil CO₂ emissions: Indonesia ≈ 690 Mt (population ≈ 278 million); Russia ≈ 1,800 Mt (≈ 144 million). World total ≈ 37,400 Mt. Calculate for each country (a) the share of world emissions and (b) emissions per capita.
items.answer: (a) Indonesia 1.84%, Russia 4.81% (b) Indonesia 2.48 t, Russia 12.50 t per person

items.stem: Using the Urgenda v the Netherlands case as an example, explain the role of litigation in climate governance.
items.answer: The Dutch Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the state must cut emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by 2020. Citizens used human-rights law to force stronger government action.
items.markingKey: Context (The Dutch Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the state must cut emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Citizens used human-rights law to force stronger government action. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of litigation in climate governance.

(a) Describe what the data show. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain the significance of the "emissions gap". [6]

items.answer: emissions trading scheme

items.answer: adaptation

items.stem: Explain why reforestation is an attractive but limited mitigation strategy.
items.answer: Trees absorb carbon and give co-benefits (biodiversity, soil, water), but they take decades to grow, need large areas that compete with food, may burn or be cleared, and cannot offset fossil emissions alone.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Trees absorb carbon and give co-benefits (biodiversity, soil, water), but they take decades to grow, need large areas that compete with food, may burn or be cleared, and cannot offset fossil emissions alone. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why poorer communities often have less capacity to adapt.
items.answer: They lack money, insurance, technology and access to credit and information; governments may be unable to fund infrastructure; livelihoods depend on climate-sensitive resources.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They lack money, insurance, technology and access to credit and information; governments may be unable to fund infrastructure; livelihoods depend on climate-sensitive resources. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why global climate agreements are difficult to achieve.
items.answer: Climate is a global commons with free-rider problems; countries differ in responsibility, wealth and vulnerability; fossil-fuel interests resist; decisions require consensus among nearly 200 parties.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Climate is a global commons with free-rider problems; countries differ in responsibility, wealth and vulnerability; fossil-fuel interests resist; decisions require consensus among nearly 200 parties. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an emissions trading scheme and a carbon tax.
items.answer: A carbon tax fixes the price of carbon and lets emissions adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the permit price adjust.
items.markingKey: A carbon tax fixes the price of carbon and lets emissions adjust; a cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the permit price adjust. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between hard adaptation measures and soft adaptation measures.
items.answer: Hard measures are engineered structures such as sea walls and embankments; soft measures include early warnings, land-use planning, insurance, ecosystem restoration and education.
items.markingKey: Hard measures are engineered structures such as sea walls and embankments; soft measures include early warnings, land-use planning, insurance, ecosystem restoration and education. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: Kyoto set legally binding targets only for industrialised countries (top-down); Paris requires all parties to submit voluntary, self-determined NDCs with binding procedures for reporting (bottom-up).
items.markingKey: Kyoto set legally binding targets only for industrialised countries (top-down); Paris requires all parties to submit voluntary, self-determined NDCs with binding procedures for reporting (bottom-up). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the Great Green Wall in the Sahel as an example, explain the opportunities and limits of reforestation.
items.answer: Launched in 2007 to restore 100 million ha across 11 countries, but only a small fraction had been restored by 2020. Large-scale tree planting brings carbon and livelihood benefits but faces funding, survival and governance problems.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in 2007 to restore 100 million ha across 11 countries, but only a small fraction had been restored by 2020.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large-scale tree planting brings carbon and livelihood benefits but faces funding, survival and governance problems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the opportunities and limits of reforestation.

items.stem: Tide-gauge records at Funafuti, Tuvalu show mean sea level of 7091 mm (relative to a local datum) in 1990 and 7210 mm in 2010. Calculate the mean rate of relative sea-level rise. Project the additional rise over the next 75 years at this rate, and explain why the rate here may differ from the global mean (about 3.7 mm/yr recently).
items.answer: 6.0 mm/yr; ≈ 45 cm in 75 years; local subsidence (groundwater pumping, delta compaction), tectonics or ocean circulation alter relative rise.
items.markingKey: A1 6.0 mm/yr; A1 446 mm; R1 R1 relative vs eustatic explanation.

items.stem: Outline two strengths and one weakness of the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: Strengths: near-universal participation; a clear temperature goal and five-yearly ratchet. Weakness: pledges are voluntary and insufficient for 1.5 °C; no enforcement mechanism.
items.markingKey: Strengths: near-universal participation; a clear temperature goal and five-yearly ratchet. Weakness: pledges are voluntary and insufficient for 1.5 °C; no enforcement mechanism.

items.stem: A cement plant covered by South Africa emits 506,000 t CO₂ per year. The carbon price is about ZAR 190 per tonne. Calculate the annual carbon cost, and the saving if the plant cuts emissions by 25%.
items.answer: cost ZAR 96,140,000; after cut ZAR 72,105,000; saving ZAR 24,035,000

items.stem: Suggest why Rotterdam is considered a world leader in climate adaptation.
items.answer: It combines hard defences (Maeslantkering barrier) with water squares that store storm water, green roofs, floating pavilions and planning to be "climate proof".
items.markingKey: It combines hard defences (Maeslantkering barrier) with water squares that store storm water, green roofs, floating pavilions and planning to be "climate proof".

items.stem: Briefly describe COP28 in Dubai (2023) and explain what it reveals about the slow progress of international negotiations.
items.answer: Parties agreed for the first time to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems". Consensus decisions produce compromise wording rather than a clear phase-out.

Calculate the percentage of electricity from renewable sources. Also calculate the share from fossil fuels and the share that is low-carbon (renewables + nuclear).
items.answer: Total 618 TWh; renewables 272 TWh = 44.0%; fossil 39.2%; low-carbon 60.8%

items.answer: Carbon pricing is highly effective where politically sustainable, but it works best with regulation and public investment.

items.stem: Which country introduced one of the world's first carbon taxes in 1991, now among the highest at about SEK 1,200 per tonne?
items.answer: Sweden
items.markingKey: C. Sweden cut emissions by about a third while its economy grew.

items.stem: Approximately how many cyclone shelters has Bangladesh built along its coast?
items.answer: About 4,000 or more
items.markingKey: B. Shelters plus the Cyclone Preparedness Programme volunteers have cut cyclone deaths sharply.

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement, how often should countries submit updated NDCs?
items.answer: Every five years
items.markingKey: A. The "ratchet mechanism" aims to increase ambition over time.

items.stem: A student claims: "Geo-engineering would solve climate change, so emissions cuts are unnecessary." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Solar geo-engineering would mask warming but not remove CO₂, leaving ocean acidification and the risk of rapid warming if it stopped.
items.markingKey: Solar geo-engineering would mask warming but not remove CO₂, leaving ocean acidification and the risk of rapid warming if it stopped. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between soft adaptation measures and hard adaptation measures.
items.answer: Hard measures are engineered structures such as sea walls and embankments; soft measures include early warnings, land-use planning, insurance, ecosystem restoration and education.
items.markingKey: Hard measures are engineered structures such as sea walls and embankments; soft measures include early warnings, land-use planning, insurance, ecosystem restoration and education. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between state actors and non-state actors in climate governance.
items.answer: State actors are national governments negotiating treaties; non-state actors include cities, businesses, NGOs and social movements that act and lobby independently.
items.markingKey: State actors are national governments negotiating treaties; non-state actors include cities, businesses, NGOs and social movements that act and lobby independently. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between adaptation and mitigation.
items.answer: Mitigation tackles the causes of climate change by reducing emissions or increasing sinks; adaptation reduces the harm from climate impacts that cannot be avoided.
items.markingKey: Mitigation tackles the causes of climate change by reducing emissions or increasing sinks; adaptation reduces the harm from climate impacts that cannot be avoided. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Building higher sea walls is always the best adaptation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Sea walls are expensive, can fail, push erosion elsewhere and encourage development in risky places (maladaptation); soft or nature-based options may be better.
items.markingKey: Sea walls are expensive, can fail, push erosion elsewhere and encourage development in risky places (maladaptation); soft or nature-based options may be better. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why cities are becoming important actors in climate governance.
items.answer: Cities produce about 70% of energy-related CO₂, control transport, buildings and planning, and networks such as C40 allow them to act faster than national governments.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cities produce about 70% of energy-related CO₂, control transport, buildings and planning, and networks such as C40 allow them to act faster than national governments.
